entries.meaning: After noon — used after a time between noon and midnight. ---
examples: The store closes at 9 p.m.
My flight lands at 6:45 p.m. Eastern time.
Office hours are 1 to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday.
entries.type: time — after noon, with a clock time
entries.position: after its word — after the number
entries.form: abbreviation of Latin post meridiem, after noon
entries.contrast: Americans use the 12-hour clock where Russian uses 19:00: say 7 p.m. Use it only after a number: not in the p.m., not 7 o'clock p.m., and not 7 p.m. in the evening (the evening is already in p.m.). 12 p.m. is noon, which confuses people, so say noon or midnight.

entries.meaning: Painfully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The line at the DMV moved painfully slowly.
She was painfully shy as a child.
It was painfully obvious that he hadn't read the book.
He fell painfully on his elbow.
Her knee was still painfully swollen.

senses.head: Very, to an unpleasant degree — often with slow, shy, aware or obvious
examples: The line at the DMV moved painfully slowly.
She was painfully shy as a child.
It was painfully obvious that he hadn't read the book.

senses.head: In a way that causes physical or emotional pain
examples: He fell painfully on his elbow.
Her knee was still painfully swollen.

entries.position: before its word — or end when it means with pain

entries.meaning: Without pain, or without trouble or difficulty. ---
examples: The tooth came out quickly and painlessly.
The switch to the new software went painlessly.
You can renew your license painlessly online.

entries.meaning: With great care and attention to every detail. ---
examples: The old car was painstakingly restored.
She painstakingly checked every number in the report.
They rebuilt the bridge painstakingly, stone by stone.
entries.position: mid or end — also before a participle (painstakingly restored)

entries.meaning: So clearly that it can almost be touched or felt. ---
examples: The crowd was palpably nervous before the final shot.
The claim is palpably false.
The mood in the office has palpably changed since the layoffs.
entries.type: degree — so strongly it can almost be felt

entries.meaning: In a way that seems to contradict itself or what you would expect. ---
examples: Paradoxically, the more choices people have, the less happy they feel.
The drug is paradoxically more effective at lower doses.
The quietest kid in class was, paradoxically, the best public speaker.
entries.type: stance — the opposite of what you would expect

entries.meaning: As an extra remark, added in passing. ---
examples: She mentioned, almost parenthetically, that she was moving to Chicago.
Parenthetically, I should add that the data is from 2019.
The author notes parenthetically that the study was never repeated.
entries.modifies: verbs of saying and whole clauses

entries.meaning: Partly; to some extent — often in pairs. ---
examples: The creature was part man, part wolf.
The trip was part business, part vacation.
Her dog is part husky.
entries.position: before its word — usually in pairs (part …, part …)
entries.contrast: Part is usually a noun (a part of the plan). As an adverb it comes before a noun or adjective, most often in pairs: part man, part wolf. Before a single adjective, partly sounds more natural: partly true.

entries.meaning: For only part of the normal working or study hours. ---
examples: She works part-time at a bookstore.
He's studying part-time while he raises two kids.
Many students work part-time to pay for college.
entries.type: duration — for only part of the usual working hours
entries.contrast: Adverb after a verb: She works part-time. Adjective before a noun: a part-time job. The opposite is full-time.

entries.meaning: Fairly; well enough to be acceptable. ---
examples: He speaks passably good Spanish.
The food was passably decent for an airport.
She plays the guitar passably well.
entries.type: degree — well enough, but not very well

entries.meaning: With strong feeling or great enthusiasm. ---
examples: She spoke passionately about climate change.
They kissed passionately at the airport.
He believes passionately that everyone deserves a second chance.

entries.meaning: Without taking action or resisting; just accepting what happens. ---
examples: Don't just sit passively and wait for things to change.
Most people watch TV passively.
She passively accepted whatever her boss said.

entries.meaning: Pat has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She practiced her speech until she had it down pat.
It took me a month to get the dance steps down pat.
The Fed is expected to stand pat on interest rates this month.
Despite the losing streak, the team stood pat at the trade deadline.

senses.head: Perfectly, learned by heart — in have or get something down pat
examples: She practiced her speech until she had it down pat.
It took me a month to get the dance steps down pat.

senses.head: Without changing anything — in stand pat, keep a decision or position
examples: The Fed is expected to stand pat on interest rates this month.
Despite the losing streak, the team stood pat at the trade deadline.

entries.type: manner — only in down pat and stand pat
entries.modifies: down in have something down pat, and stand in stand pat
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective pat
entries.contrast: The adjective before a noun is critical: a pat answer is a quick, rehearsed reply (шаблонный, заученный ответ). The verb and noun pat mean похлопать, похлопывание: pat the dog. Stand pat comes from poker and is mainly American.

entries.meaning: Very clearly; in a way nobody can doubt. ---
examples: That claim is patently false.
It was patently obvious that she didn't want to go.
The rule is patently unfair to part-time workers.
entries.type: degree — obviously, usually with a negative adjective
entries.form: -ly from patent in the sense obvious

entries.meaning: Pathetically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The pay is pathetically low.
Our team played pathetically in the second half.
He was pathetically grateful for any attention.
The puppy whimpered pathetically outside the door.
She looked up at me pathetically and asked for help.

senses.head: So badly or so little that it deserves pity or scorn
examples: The pay is pathetically low.
Our team played pathetically in the second half.
He was pathetically grateful for any attention.

senses.head: In a sad way that makes people feel sorry for you
examples: The puppy whimpered pathetically outside the door.
She looked up at me pathetically and asked for help.

entries.contrast: False friend: pathetically is not патетически (with pathos, grandly). It means жалко or жалобно, and often shows contempt: pathetically low pay. For патетически use with great emotion or grandly.

entries.meaning: To an extreme degree that seems like an illness. ---
examples: He's pathologically afraid of flying.
She's pathologically shy around strangers.
My boss is pathologically unable to admit a mistake.
entries.type: degree — to an extreme, unhealthy degree

entries.meaning: Calmly, without getting annoyed or in a hurry. ---
examples: We waited patiently for our turn.
She patiently explained the rules again.
The teacher listened patiently to every excuse.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows love for and loyalty to your country. ---
examples: The whole street was patriotically decorated for the Fourth of July.
They sang the anthem patriotically, hands on their hearts.
He patriotically joined the army after the attack.
entries.position: mid or end — also before a participle (patriotically decorated)

entries.meaning: In a way that treats someone as less intelligent or important than you. ---
examples: He smiled patronizingly and said I'd understand when I was older.
Don't talk to me so patronizingly.
She patronizingly explained how to use a microwave.

entries.meaning: Without fighting or causing trouble. ---
examples: The protesters gathered peaceably outside city hall.
The two sides settled the dispute peaceably.
The First Amendment protects the right of the people peaceably to assemble.
entries.contrast: Peaceably stresses behaving without fighting and sounds formal or legal (the First Amendment's peaceably to assemble). Peacefully is the everyday word and also means calmly, quietly: sleeping peacefully, never sleeping peaceably.

entries.meaning: Peacefully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The protest ended peacefully.
The two countries resolved the conflict peacefully.
The baby was sleeping peacefully in her crib.
He died peacefully at home, surrounded by family.

senses.head: Without violence or fighting
examples: The protest ended peacefully.
The two countries resolved the conflict peacefully.

senses.head: Calmly and quietly
examples: The baby was sleeping peacefully in her crib.
He died peacefully at home, surrounded by family.

entries.meaning: Peculiarly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's been acting peculiarly all week.
The streets were peculiarly quiet for a Saturday night.
It's a peculiarly American way of thinking about money.
The problem is peculiarly difficult for small towns.

senses.head: In a strange or unusual way
examples: He's been acting peculiarly all week.
The streets were peculiarly quiet for a Saturday night.

senses.head: Especially; in a way typical of one person, place or group
examples: It's a peculiarly American way of thinking about money.
The problem is peculiarly difficult for small towns.

entries.meaning: In terms of teaching and how people learn. ---
examples: The method is pedagogically sound but hard to use in large classes.
Pedagogically, it makes more sense to teach listening before grammar.
The textbook is pedagogically outdated.
entries.type: viewpoint — from the point of view of teaching

entries.meaning: In a way that is too concerned with small details or rules. ---
examples: "Technically, a tomato is a fruit," he said pedantically.
She pedantically corrected every comma in my email.
Don't be so pedantically literal about the rules.
entries.contrast: Russian педантичный is often praise (аккуратный, пунктуальный). English pedantic and pedantically are criticism: too concerned with small rules and details, showing off knowledge. For praise use meticulously or carefully.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows disapproval or a low opinion. ---
examples: The word "nerd" was once used only pejoratively.
Some people use "millennial" pejoratively.
She didn't mean "ambitious" pejoratively; it was a compliment.
entries.type: manner — about how a word or name is used
entries.position: end — usually after used or called
entries.modifies: verbs of using and naming (use, call, refer to)

entries.meaning: In a hurried, confused and disorderly way. ---
examples: The kids ran pell-mell out of the school when the bell rang.
Clothes were thrown pell-mell into the suitcase.
The crowd rushed pell-mell toward the exits.
entries.modifies: verbs of movement (run, rush) and throw

entries.meaning: In a quiet, thoughtful way, often a little sad. ---
examples: She stared pensively out the window.
He stroked his beard pensively.
"I'm not sure," she said pensively.

entries.meaning: For each person in a population. ---
examples: The US spends more on health care per capita than any other country.
The state collects about $3,000 in taxes per capita.
Coffee consumption per capita is highest in Finland.
entries.type: manner — for each person, in statistics
entries.modifies: verbs of spending, earning, using; numbers
entries.contrast: Before a noun it works as an adjective: per capita income. As an adverb it follows the verb or figure: spends more per capita.

entries.meaning: By itself; in its own nature, apart from other things. ---
examples: Money per se doesn't make people happy.
I'm not against the plan per se, just the timing.
The drug isn't dangerous per se.
entries.position: after its word — right after the noun, or at the end
entries.modifies: a noun or a whole statement, often negative

entries.meaning: Enough to be noticed. ---
examples: The temperature dropped perceptibly after sunset.
Her voice was perceptibly shaky.
Traffic hasn't improved perceptibly since the new lanes opened.
entries.contrast: Do not mix up perceptibly (noticeably, заметно) and perceptively (with insight, проницательно).

entries.meaning: With a quick and deep understanding of people or situations. ---
examples: The critic writes perceptively about family relationships.
She perceptively noticed that something was wrong.
He commented perceptively on the weaknesses of the plan.
entries.contrast: Do not mix up perceptively (with insight, проницательно) and perceptibly (noticeably, заметно).

entries.meaning: In a sudden, commanding way that allows no discussion. ---
examples: The judge peremptorily dismissed the case.
She waved him away peremptorily.
He was peremptorily fired without any explanation.

entries.meaning: Always, or again and again over many years. ---
examples: It's a perennially popular vacation spot.
Parking is a perennially sore subject in this town.
The team is perennially at the bottom of the league.
entries.русский: постоянно, вечно, из года в год

entries.meaning: Quickly and without real interest or care, only because you have to. ---
examples: The guard checked our IDs perfunctorily and waved us through.
She smiled perfunctorily and went back to her phone.
He perfunctorily apologized and changed the subject.

entries.meaning: Dangerously; in a way that could easily lead to disaster. ---
examples: The car stopped perilously close to the edge of the cliff.
The company came perilously close to bankruptcy.
The ladder leaned perilously against the wall.
entries.type: degree — dangerously, most often in perilously close

entries.meaning: Only in a minor way, not at the center of something. ---
examples: I was only peripherally involved in the project.
The book deals with the war only peripherally.
That issue is only peripherally related to what we're discussing.
entries.type: degree — only slightly, at the edges
entries.position: before its word — often after only

entries.meaning: At a right angle to something, or straight up. ---
examples: The two streets run perpendicularly to each other.
Cut the board perpendicularly to the grain.
The cliff rises almost perpendicularly from the sea.

entries.meaning: All the time, or so often that it seems like all the time. ---
examples: My brother is perpetually late.
She seems perpetually tired these days.
The printer is perpetually out of ink.

entries.meaning: Persistently has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He persistently asked for a raise until they gave him one.
Reporters questioned her persistently about the scandal.
Unemployment has remained persistently high.
Children who are persistently absent fall behind.

senses.head: Again and again, refusing to give up
examples: He persistently asked for a raise until they gave him one.
Reporters questioned her persistently about the scandal.

senses.head: For a long time, without stopping or improving
examples: Unemployment has remained persistently high.
Children who are persistently absent fall behind.

entries.meaning: In a way that makes people believe or agree. ---
examples: She argued persuasively for a four-day workweek.
The article makes the case persuasively.
He writes clearly and persuasively.

entries.meaning: Perversely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Perversely, the price went up as demand fell.
The long delay perversely made the fans even more excited.
She perversely turned down the job everyone told her to take.
He perversely enjoys arguing with people who agree with him.

senses.head: Strangely, in a way that is the opposite of what you would expect
examples: Perversely, the price went up as demand fell.
The long delay perversely made the fans even more excited.

senses.head: Deliberately doing the opposite of what is wanted or reasonable
examples: She perversely turned down the job everyone told her to take.
He perversely enjoys arguing with people who agree with him.

entries.русский: как ни странно; назло, из упрямства
entries.position: mid — or front as a comment on the whole sentence
entries.contrast: Usually not извращённо: perversely most often means against what you would expect or want. Perversely, sales went up = как ни странно, продажи выросли.

entries.meaning: In a way that expects bad things to happen. ---
examples: Economists view the next quarter pessimistically.
"We'll never finish on time," he said pessimistically.
She pessimistically predicted that the repairs would take six months.

entries.meaning: In a bad-tempered, childish way, like someone who didn't get what they wanted. ---
examples: "I don't want to go," the boy said petulantly.
She petulantly slammed the door.
He tossed his phone petulantly onto the couch.

entries.meaning: Extremely; to an amazing degree. ---
examples: The app has been phenomenally successful.
She's a phenomenally talented singer.
The show did phenomenally well in its first season.

entries.meaning: Philosophically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He took the news of the layoffs philosophically.
"Well, that's life," she said philosophically.
Philosophically, the two thinkers had a lot in common.
The question is philosophically interesting but hard to test.

senses.head: Calmly, accepting something bad that cannot be changed
examples: He took the news of the layoffs philosophically.
"Well, that's life," she said philosophically.

senses.head: From the point of view of philosophy
examples: Philosophically, the two thinkers had a lot in common.
The question is philosophically interesting but hard to test.

entries.position: end — or front for the viewpoint sense
entries.modifies: verbs (take, accept, say), adjectives and whole clauses

entries.meaning: According to the sounds of speech, or the way a word is pronounced. ---
examples: Write the name phonetically so I know how to say it.
Young kids often spell words phonetically, like "nite" for "night."
The two words are phonetically identical but spelled differently.

entries.meaning: In terms of how living bodies work. ---
examples: Fear and excitement are physiologically very similar.
Physiologically, the body can survive only a few days without water.
Babies are physiologically ready for solid food at about six months.
entries.type: viewpoint — in terms of how the body works

entries.meaning: A little at a time, not as a whole or according to a plan. ---
examples: The old house was renovated piecemeal over ten years.
Information came out piecemeal, one leak at a time.
Don't fix the problems piecemeal; we need a real plan.
entries.form: compound of piece and old -meal, by portions
entries.contrast: Also an adjective before a noun, often critical: a piecemeal approach (бессистемный подход).

entries.meaning: Sharply and intensely, as if cutting through something. ---
examples: She screamed piercingly when she saw the snake.
He had piercingly blue eyes.
The wind off the lake was piercingly cold.
entries.modifies: adjectives (piercingly cold, piercingly blue) and verbs of sound

entries.meaning: On someone's back, with arms around their neck. ---
examples: The little girl rode piggyback on her dad.
He carried his son piggyback all the way home.
The kids took turns riding piggyback.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (give me a piggyback, a piggyback ride) and a verb meaning to use something that already exists: piggyback on someone's idea.

entries.meaning: Piously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The old woman prayed piously every morning.
They bowed their heads piously during the blessing.
Politicians talk piously about family values.
He piously reminded us that he never drinks.

senses.head: In a deeply religious way
examples: The old woman prayed piously every morning.
They bowed their heads piously during the blessing.

senses.head: In a way that shows off how morally good you think you are
examples: Politicians talk piously about family values.
He piously reminded us that he never drinks.

entries.meaning: Very — used only in piping hot, about food or drink. ---
examples: The pizza came out of the oven piping hot.
Serve the soup piping hot.
Make sure the chicken is piping hot all the way through.
entries.русский: обжигающе, с пылу с жару (только piping hot)
entries.type: degree — very, only in piping hot
entries.position: before its word — only before hot
entries.contrast: The adverb exists only in piping hot. Elsewhere piping is a noun (трубы; кант на одежде) or a form of the verb pipe.

entries.meaning: In a short, clever way that says a lot in few words. ---
examples: As one critic pithily put it, the movie is all trailer and no film.
She summed up the problem pithily: too many meetings, not enough work.
The review was pithily written and very funny.
entries.modifies: verbs of saying and writing (put, sum up, write)

entries.meaning: Pitifully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The pay was pitifully low.
Pitifully few people showed up to vote.
The kitten mewed pitifully in the rain.
He limped pitifully back to the bench.

senses.head: Sadly or shamefully too little — often with small, few or low
examples: The pay was pitifully low.
Pitifully few people showed up to vote.

senses.head: In a way that makes people feel pity
examples: The kitten mewed pitifully in the rain.
He limped pitifully back to the bench.

entries.modifies: adjectives (pitifully small, pitifully few) and verbs

entries.meaning: Calmly, without excitement or disturbance. ---
examples: Cows grazed placidly in the field.
She smiled placidly, as if nothing had happened.
The lake lay placidly under the morning fog.

entries.meaning: Simply; completely — for emphasis. ---
examples: That's just plain wrong.
He's not shy; he's plain rude.
Some people are just plain lucky.
entries.type: degree — informal, before a negative adjective
entries.position: before its word — often after just (just plain wrong)
entries.modifies: adjectives, especially negative ones (wrong, rude, stupid)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective plain
entries.contrast: Informal and mostly American, usually with just: just plain wrong. Don't confuse it with the adjective plain (simple, without decoration: a plain shirt) or with plainly (clearly: plainly visible).

entries.meaning: Plainly has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He was plainly upset about the news.
Plainly, something has to change.
The sign was plainly visible from the road.
Let me put it plainly: you're fired.
She spoke plainly about her illness.
The room was plainly furnished.
He was dressed plainly in jeans and a T-shirt.

senses.head: Clearly; obviously
examples: He was plainly upset about the news.
Plainly, something has to change.
The sign was plainly visible from the road.

senses.head: Directly and honestly, in simple words
examples: Let me put it plainly: you're fired.
She spoke plainly about her illness.

senses.head: Simply, without decoration
examples: The room was plainly furnished.
He was dressed plainly in jeans and a T-shirt.

entries.meaning: In a sad, high sound, as if asking for sympathy. ---
examples: The dog whined plaintively at the door.
"Can't we stay a little longer?" she asked plaintively.
A train whistle sounded plaintively in the distance.

entries.meaning: In a way that seems reasonable or likely to be true. ---
examples: He argued plausibly that the fire was an accident.
The story could plausibly be true.
She explained plausibly why she was late.

entries.meaning: In a fun, joking way, not seriously. ---
examples: She punched him playfully on the arm.
The puppies wrestled playfully on the rug.
"Maybe I will, maybe I won't," he said playfully.

entries.meaning: In a way that begs for something. ---
examples: The kids looked at their mom pleadingly.
"Please don't tell anyone," he said pleadingly.
The dog stared pleadingly at my sandwich.

entries.meaning: Pleasantly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I was pleasantly surprised by how good the food was.
The evening was pleasantly cool.
The receptionist smiled pleasantly and asked us to wait.
He greeted everyone pleasantly at the door.

senses.head: In a way that is enjoyable or nice
examples: I was pleasantly surprised by how good the food was.
The evening was pleasantly cool.

senses.head: In a friendly, polite way
examples: The receptionist smiled pleasantly and asked us to wait.
He greeted everyone pleasantly at the door.

entries.modifies: adjectives and past participles (pleasantly surprised), verbs

entries.meaning: Used to make a request polite, or to accept an offer (Yes, please). ---
examples: Can I have a glass of water, please?
Please don't park in front of the garage.
"Would you like some coffee?" "Yes, please."
entries.position: any position — usually at the start or end of a request
entries.modifies: requests, commands and replies to offers
entries.contrast: Russian пожалуйста does jobs please can't. After thank you, say You're welcome, not Please. When handing something over, say Here you go. To accept an offer, say Yes, please. Please doesn't make a bare command fully polite: Could you close the door, please? is softer than Close the door, please. As a verb, please means радовать, угождать: She's hard to please.

entries.meaning: In a way that gives pleasure or satisfaction. ---
examples: The design is simple and pleasingly modern.
The colors blend together pleasingly.
The novel is pleasingly short.

entries.meaning: Very or more than enough — informal. ---
examples: The room is plenty big enough for two beds.
It's plenty warm in here, so turn off the heater.
Trust me, he's plenty smart.
entries.position: before its word — an adjective, often with enough
entries.modifies: adjectives and adjectives + enough (plenty big enough)
entries.contrast: Plenty is usually a pronoun: plenty of time (много, достаточно времени). The adverb, straight before an adjective, is informal American: It's plenty warm, never plenty of warm. In formal writing use quite or more than: more than big enough.

entries.meaning: Poetically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She writes poetically about the desert.
He described their first meeting poetically.
The sun set, poetically, just as the song ended.
Poetically, he hit a home run in the last game before he retired.

senses.head: In a beautiful, expressive way, like poetry
examples: She writes poetically about the desert.
He described their first meeting poetically.

senses.head: Fittingly, in a way so neat it seems planned, as in a story
examples: The sun set, poetically, just as the song ended.
Poetically, he hit a home run in the last game before he retired.

entries.position: end — or front and between commas for the fitting sense

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you feel sad or deeply moved. ---
examples: The film poignantly captures the pain of losing a parent.
Her letter was poignantly simple.
The song ends poignantly with a single piano note.
entries.position: mid or end — or before an adjective

entries.meaning: Point-blank has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I asked him point-blank whether he was quitting.
She refused point-blank to sign the contract.
He told me point-blank that my plan wouldn't work.
The officer was shot point-blank in the chest.
The goalie stopped a shot fired almost point-blank.

senses.head: Directly and bluntly, without explaining or softening anything
examples: I asked him point-blank whether he was quitting.
She refused point-blank to sign the contract.
He told me point-blank that my plan wouldn't work.

senses.head: From very close range — of a shot
examples: The officer was shot point-blank in the chest.
The goalie stopped a shot fired almost point-blank.

entries.type: manner — bluntly and directly; also of a shot fired from very close
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object (asked him point-blank)
entries.modifies: verbs of saying, asking and refusing; verbs of shooting
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective in point-blank range

entries.meaning: In a way that makes a meaning or feeling very clear, often a critical one. ---
examples: She pointedly ignored his question and turned to me.
"Some of us were on time," he said, looking pointedly at his watch.
The governor pointedly did not mention the mayor in her speech.
entries.type: manner — in a way meant to be noticed

entries.meaning: Without any purpose or useful result. ---
examples: We sat in traffic pointlessly for an hour before turning around.
The meeting dragged on pointlessly until noon.
Thousands of soldiers died pointlessly in that battle.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows good manners and respect for other people. ---
examples: The waiter politely asked us to lower our voices.
She politely declined the invitation.
Could you ask him a little more politely next time?

entries.meaning: In a self-important way, as if you were more important or wiser than others. ---
examples: He pompously informed us that he had read every book on the subject.
The senator spoke pompously about his own achievements.
"I never make mistakes," she announced pompously.

entries.meaning: In a slow, heavy, awkward way; or in a dull, overly serious way. ---
examples: The old elephant moved ponderously toward the water.
The loaded truck climbed ponderously up the hill.
The book is ponderously written and hard to finish.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or participle (ponderously written)
entries.modifies: verbs of moving, speaking and writing; participles

entries.meaning: Badly; not well or not enough. ---
examples: He did poorly on the math test.
The room was cold and poorly lit.
Most of the workers there are poorly paid.
entries.position: end — also before a past participle (poorly paid)
entries.modifies: verbs and past participles (poorly written, poorly lit)

entries.meaning: By most people, or by people in general rather than experts or officials. ---
examples: The disease is popularly known as mad cow disease.
It is popularly believed that we only use ten percent of our brains.
In many states, judges are popularly elected.
entries.position: before its word — usually before a past participle (popularly known as)

entries.meaning: In a way that seems to warn of something important or bad, often too seriously or pompously. ---
examples: "Things are about to change," he said portentously.
Dark clouds gathered portentously over the hills.
The film opens portentously, with slow music and a voice-over about fate.

entries.meaning: Positively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Customers have responded positively to the new design.
Try to think positively about the interview.
Regular exercise affects your mood positively.
The food there is positively awful.
The kids were positively bouncing off the walls.
The police have positively identified the driver.

senses.head: In a good, approving or hopeful way
examples: Customers have responded positively to the new design.
Try to think positively about the interview.
Regular exercise affects your mood positively.

senses.head: Completely; really; with certainty — used to add emphasis
examples: The food there is positively awful.
The kids were positively bouncing off the walls.
The police have positively identified the driver.

entries.type: manner; also degree — as an intensifier
entries.position: any position — end in the manner sense (respond positively); before an adjective or verb as an intensifier (positively awful)
entries.comparison: more/most — in the first sense only
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives and verbs as an intensifier
entries.contrast: After test and come back, English uses the adjective: She tested positive for COVID (положительный результат), not tested positively. The intensifier sense has nothing to do with good news: positively awful means really awful.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you want to keep someone or something to yourself. ---
examples: He put his arm possessively around his girlfriend.
The dog guarded its bone possessively.
She clutched the remote possessively and refused to share it.

entries.meaning: As fast as possible; right away — often a little humorous or formal. ---
examples: The senator flew back to Washington posthaste.
When the boss called, he left the party posthaste.
Send the signed forms back to us posthaste.
entries.type: time — at once and in a hurry
entries.modifies: verbs of going, sending and leaving
entries.form: post (by express courier) + haste; American dictionaries write it as one word, WordNet as post-haste

entries.meaning: After a person's death. ---
examples: The soldier was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor.
Her last novel was published posthumously.
The album came out posthumously, a year after the singer died.
entries.position: end — also before a past participle (posthumously awarded)
entries.form: -ly from posthumous; the h is silent

entries.meaning: Possibly; in a way that could happen or develop in the future. ---
examples: The storm is potentially dangerous.
This mistake could potentially cost us millions.
We talked to three potentially interested buyers.
entries.position: before its word — also mid (could potentially)

entries.meaning: With great strength, force or effect. ---
examples: He's a powerfully built man with huge shoulders.
She spoke powerfully about her time in the military.
The river flows powerfully after the spring rains.
entries.position: end — also before a past participle (powerfully built)

entries.meaning: Without the power or ability to do anything about what is happening. ---
examples: We watched powerlessly as the flames spread to the roof.
Residents stood by powerlessly while the river rose.
She could only look on powerlessly as her company collapsed.
entries.position: end — mostly after watch and stand by
entries.modifies: verbs, especially watch and stand by

entries.meaning: In a practical way, based on what works rather than on theory or ideals. ---
examples: She approaches every problem pragmatically.
Pragmatically, we can't afford to hire anyone this year.
The two parties worked together pragmatically to pass the budget.
entries.position: any position — end as manner; front with a comma as viewpoint

entries.meaning: In an unsteady or unsafe way, likely to fall or fail. ---
examples: A stack of dishes was balanced precariously on the edge of the counter.
The house sits precariously on the side of a cliff.
The family lives precariously, one paycheck away from losing their home.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (precariously balanced)

entries.meaning: Very — used before little or few to stress how small an amount is. ---
examples: We have precious little time left.
Precious few people showed up to the meeting.
There's precious little evidence that the diet works.
entries.type: degree — only in precious little and precious few
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective precious
entries.contrast: As an adverb, precious works only before little and few and stresses how small an amount is: precious little time = очень мало времени. It does not mean драгоценный here.

entries.meaning: Very suddenly and steeply — usually of a fall. ---
examples: Stock prices dropped precipitously after the announcement.
The trail falls away precipitously to the river below.
Enrollment has declined precipitously over the last five years.

entries.meaning: At an unusually early age; more developed than is normal for a child. ---
examples: She was a precociously gifted pianist who performed at seven.
He read precociously, finishing Tolkien by age eight.
Their daughter talks precociously for a three-year-old.
entries.position: before its word — usually before an adjective (precociously talented); also end

entries.meaning: Mostly; mainly. ---
examples: The neighborhood is predominantly Hispanic.
Their customers are predominantly young women.
The disease occurs predominantly in older adults.
entries.position: before its word — also mid (is predominantly)
entries.modifies: adjectives, nouns, verbs and prepositional phrases

entries.meaning: If possible; as a better choice. ---
examples: Take one pill a day, preferably with food.
We're looking for someone with experience, preferably in sales.
Call me back today, preferably before five.
entries.type: stance — what the speaker would prefer
entries.position: any position — usually right before the word or phrase it applies to (preferably by Friday)
entries.form: -ly from preferable; stressed on the first syllable, like preference

entries.meaning: In a way that gives one person or thing an advantage over others. ---
examples: Some employees felt the boss treated his friends preferentially.
The hospital does not preferentially admit insured patients.
Plants take up this nutrient preferentially when the soil is wet.

entries.meaning: Too early, before the normal or expected time. ---
examples: The twins were born prematurely, at 32 weeks.
He went prematurely gray in his thirties.
The season ended prematurely because of the pandemic.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or participle (prematurely gray)

entries.meaning: Absurdly; to a degree that is ridiculous. ---
examples: The tickets were preposterously expensive.
The plot of the movie is preposterously complicated.
He made a preposterously large bet on the game.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows knowledge of what will happen before it happens. ---
examples: She presciently sold her stocks just before the market crashed.
The author presciently described smartphones in a novel from the 1980s.
As one critic presciently noted, the show would become a huge hit.

entries.meaning: In a way that looks neat and good enough for other people to see. ---
examples: Please dress presentably for the interview.
Make sure the kids are presentably dressed for dinner.
The house was presentably clean by the time the buyers arrived.

entries.meaning: In a way that assumes too much, taking a right or a liberty you do not have. ---
examples: He presumptuously invited himself to our wedding.
She presumptuously started calling the CEO by his first name.
I presumptuously assumed I'd get the job and turned down other offers.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with presumably (вероятно, надо полагать): He presumably knew = he probably knew; He presumptuously assumed he was invited = he had no right to assume it.

entries.meaning: In a way that tries to seem more important, smart or stylish than is really true. ---
examples: The restaurant's menu is pretentiously written in French.
He talked pretentiously about wine all evening.
The film is beautiful but pretentiously slow.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or participle

entries.meaning: To an unusual or almost unnatural degree. ---
examples: She stayed preternaturally calm during the crisis.
The actor looks preternaturally young for sixty.
He has a preternaturally good memory for names.

entries.meaning: Almost; very nearly. ---
examples: I'm pretty much done with the report.
The two phones are pretty much the same.
He pretty much lives at the gym.
entries.position: before its word — or mid (I pretty much agree)
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives like done or the same, all, everyone
entries.contrast: Pretty here means fairly, not beautiful. Informal; in writing use almost or nearly.

entries.meaning: In a very formal, proper way that shows you are easily shocked by anything rude. ---
examples: She sat primly on the edge of the couch with her knees together.
"We don't use that word in this house," Grandma said primly.
He smiled primly and folded his napkin.

entries.meaning: Mainly; mostly. ---
examples: The program is aimed principally at small businesses.
She is known principally as a jazz singer.
The delay was caused principally by bad weather.
entries.position: before its word — before the word or phrase it focuses on; also mid
entries.contrast: principally is not in principle (в принципе). It was built principally for kids = mainly for kids; In principle, I agree = в принципе я согласен.

entries.meaning: Privately has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Can I talk to you privately for a minute?
Privately, he admitted that the plan had failed.
She smiled, but privately she was furious.
The museum is privately owned.
The project is privately funded.
Her kids go to a privately run school.

senses.head: Not in public; with only the people involved present, or only in your own mind
examples: Can I talk to you privately for a minute?
Privately, he admitted that the plan had failed.
She smiled, but privately she was furious.

senses.head: By private people or companies, not by the government
examples: The museum is privately owned.
The project is privately funded.
Her kids go to a privately run school.

entries.position: any position — end (talk privately); front or mid (Privately, she…); before a participle (privately owned)

entries.meaning: To an unusually great degree; in an impressively large amount. ---
examples: She was a prodigiously talented young violinist.
He drank prodigiously but never seemed drunk.
The team scored prodigiously in the first half of the season.
entries.position: before its word — also end (ate prodigiously)

entries.meaning: In a way that gets useful results or a lot done. ---
examples: Working from home, I use my time more productively.
The two teams worked together productively on the launch.
Kids need a way to spend their energy productively.

entries.meaning: Professionally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He played baseball professionally for ten years.
She's a professionally trained chef.
Professionally, it was the best year of my life.
The staff handled the complaint very professionally.
Please dress professionally for the meeting.
The website looks professionally designed.

senses.head: As a job, for money, or in connection with your work
examples: He played baseball professionally for ten years.
She's a professionally trained chef.
Professionally, it was the best year of my life.

senses.head: In a skilled, correct way that meets the standards expected at work
examples: The staff handled the complaint very professionally.
Please dress professionally for the meeting.
The website looks professionally designed.

entries.position: end — also before a participle (professionally trained) and front with a comma as viewpoint

entries.meaning: With a good level of skill, from practice or training. ---
examples: She speaks Spanish and Portuguese proficiently.
All new hires must be able to use the software proficiently.
He played the violin proficiently but without much feeling.
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, using and performing

entries.meaning: In a way that makes money or brings a useful result. ---
examples: The company has operated profitably for twenty years.
They sold the house profitably after only two years.
You could spend the weekend more profitably by studying.

entries.meaning: A lot; in large amounts, often more than needed. ---
examples: He apologized profusely for being late.
She was bleeding profusely from a cut on her head.
I was sweating profusely by the end of the hike.

entries.meaning: Gradually and steadily, a little more at each stage. ---
examples: His health got progressively worse over the winter.
The questions become progressively harder.
The pain progressively spread down her arm.
entries.type: manner — step by step; also degree before comparatives (progressively worse)
entries.position: before its word — before a comparative (progressively worse); also mid

entries.meaning: So much that people cannot pay for it or do it. ---
examples: Housing in San Francisco is prohibitively expensive.
The cost of the surgery was prohibitively high.
Shipping the piano turned out to be prohibitively costly.
entries.modifies: adjectives, mostly expensive, high and costly

entries.meaning: In a place or way that is easy to see or notice; as an important part of something. ---
examples: The award is prominently displayed in the lobby.
Her photo was featured prominently on the front page.
Health care figured prominently in the debate.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (prominently displayed)

entries.meaning: Without choosing carefully; also, of sex, with many different partners. ---
examples: Doctors have prescribed antibiotics too promiscuously for decades.
The chef borrows promiscuously from Thai, Mexican and Italian cooking.
In the novel, he lives promiscuously and drinks too much.

entries.meaning: In a way that suggests things will go well. ---
examples: The season started promisingly with three straight wins.
The first round of tests went promisingly.
Her acting career began promisingly on Broadway.

entries.meaning: Promptly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Please pay your bill promptly.
The fire department responded promptly to the call.
He sat down on the couch and promptly fell asleep.
The meeting starts promptly at 9 a.m.
Class begins promptly at eight, so don't be late.

senses.head: Quickly and without delay
examples: Please pay your bill promptly.
The fire department responded promptly to the call.
He sat down on the couch and promptly fell asleep.

senses.head: Exactly at the stated time
examples: The meeting starts promptly at 9 a.m.
Class begins promptly at eight, so don't be late.

entries.position: mid or end — mid in the first sense; before a clock time in the second (promptly at nine)

entries.meaning: Immediately; right now — informal. ---
examples: Get over here, pronto!
I need that report on my desk pronto.
We'd better fix that leak pronto.

entries.meaning: Properly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Make sure the chicken is cooked properly.
The printer isn't working properly.
I haven't slept properly in days.
Sit up and behave properly at the table.
You can't go to a funeral in shorts — dress properly.

senses.head: Correctly; in the right or satisfactory way
examples: Make sure the chicken is cooked properly.
The printer isn't working properly.
I haven't slept properly in days.

senses.head: In a polite, socially acceptable way
examples: Sit up and behave properly at the table.
You can't go to a funeral in shorts — dress properly.

entries.position: end — also before a participle (properly cooked)

entries.meaning: In a way that correctly describes or warns about what will happen later. ---
examples: In 1995, he prophetically warned that the internet would change everything.
"This won't end well," she said, rather prophetically.
The report, which prophetically predicted the housing crash, was ignored.

entries.meaning: In a way that matches the size or amount of something else. ---
examples: If sales go up, the bonuses will increase proportionally.
Divide the cost proportionally among the three families.
Rural areas are not proportionally represented in the survey.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or participle

entries.meaning: In a way that matches the size, amount or seriousness of something else. ---
examples: The punishment should be proportionately severe.
Taxes on the rich have not risen proportionately.
Small towns lost proportionately more jobs than big cities.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or comparative
entries.form: -ly from proportionate; means the same as proportionally

entries.meaning: In an ordinary, unexciting way; without imagination or romance. ---
examples: The ship was prosaically named Cargo Carrier 7.
Some call it fate; more prosaically, it was a scheduling mistake.
She explained, rather prosaically, that the ghost was just a leaky pipe.
entries.position: any position — end as manner; front with a comma, often more prosaically

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you want to keep someone or something safe. ---
examples: She wrapped her arms protectively around her son.
The dog stood protectively in front of the baby.
He held his injured hand protectively against his chest.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are proud. ---
examples: She proudly showed us her diploma.
The flag was flying proudly over the school.
We're a proudly family-owned business.

entries.meaning: In a way that can be shown to be true with facts or evidence. ---
examples: The claim in the ad is provably false.
Several of his statements turned out to be provably wrong.
Engineers want a system that is provably secure.
entries.type: manner — in a way that can be proved
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (provably false)
entries.modifies: adjectives, mainly false, true, wrong, secure

entries.meaning: For the present time only, until something is made final. ---
examples: The plan has been provisionally approved by the city.
The trial is provisionally set for March.
She accepted the offer provisionally, pending a background check.
entries.position: mid or end — also before a participle (provisionally approved)

entries.meaning: In a way meant to cause a strong reaction, such as anger, argument or sexual interest. ---
examples: The article is provocatively titled "Why College Is a Waste of Money."
She dressed provocatively for the party.
He argued provocatively that the city should ban cars downtown.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (provocatively titled)

entries.meaning: Carefully and sensibly, avoiding unnecessary risks. ---
examples: They prudently saved money for emergencies.
The company acted prudently by cutting costs early.
We prudently left before the storm hit.

entries.meaning: In a way that concerns the mind and emotions. ---
examples: The long isolation was psychologically damaging.
Psychologically, losing a job can be as hard as a divorce.
Players have to be psychologically ready for the playoffs.
entries.type: viewpoint; also manner — in terms of the mind
entries.position: any position — front with a comma as viewpoint; before an adjective (psychologically damaging)
entries.form: -ly from psychological; the p is silent

entries.meaning: Publicly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The senator publicly apologized for his comments.
She has never talked publicly about her divorce.
The results will be announced publicly next week.
Most American kids attend publicly funded schools.
The hospital is publicly owned by the county.

senses.head: In front of other people; openly, so that everyone knows
examples: The senator publicly apologized for his comments.
She has never talked publicly about her divorce.
The results will be announced publicly next week.

senses.head: By the government or with public money, not by private owners
examples: Most American kids attend publicly funded schools.
The hospital is publicly owned by the county.

entries.position: end — also mid and before a participle (publicly funded)
entries.contrast: The spelling is publicly, not publically — one of the few -ic adjectives that do not add -ally.

entries.meaning: In an aggressive way, ready to argue or fight. ---
examples: The candidate answered the reporters' questions pugnaciously.
He pugnaciously defended every decision he had made.
The little dog barked pugnaciously at the mail carrier.

entries.meaning: With very great care about details, rules or correct behavior. ---
examples: She punctiliously answered every letter she received.
The accountant followed the rules punctiliously.
He was punctiliously polite, even to people he disliked.
entries.contrast: Not punctually. punctiliously = with great care about details and rules (скрупулёзно, пунктуально in the sense of exact); punctually = on time (вовремя).

entries.meaning: At exactly the right or agreed time; not late. ---
examples: The train left punctually at 7:15.
She always pays her rent punctually.
The guests arrived punctually at six.
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian пунктуально can also mean careful and precise, but English punctually is only about time — arrive punctually. For careful, exact work say meticulously or carefully.

entries.meaning: With a strong, sharp smell or taste; or, of words, in a sharp, biting way. ---
examples: The kitchen smelled pungently of garlic and vinegar.
The cheese is pungently flavored and not for everyone.
The columnist writes pungently about politics.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (pungently scented)
entries.modifies: verbs of smelling and writing; participles

entries.meaning: Extremely, in a way that is very hard to bear. ---
examples: It was a punishingly hot day in Phoenix.
The training schedule is punishingly hard.
Rents in the city have become punishingly high.
entries.modifies: adjectives such as hot, hard, long, expensive

entries.meaning: In a way meant to punish, or so severe that it feels like punishment. ---
examples: Critics say the school treats minor mistakes too punitively.
Late fees on the loan were punitively high.
The law was applied punitively against protesters.
entries.type: manner; also degree — before an adjective (punitively high)

entries.meaning: According to what people say or claim, though it may not be true. ---
examples: The video purportedly shows the robbery in progress.
Police found a note purportedly written by the victim.
The pill purportedly helps you lose weight while you sleep.
entries.type: stance — reporting a claim the speaker does not vouch for
entries.position: mid — also before a participle or adjective (a note purportedly written by)
entries.modifies: verbs, participles, adjectives and whole clauses

entries.meaning: With a clear aim and determination. ---
examples: She strode purposefully across the parking lot.
He picked up the phone and dialed purposefully.
The new mayor has acted quickly and purposefully.
entries.contrast: purposefully = with a clear aim and determination: She walked purposefully toward the door (решительно). purposely = on purpose: He purposely left the door open (нарочно). Many Americans also use purposefully to mean on purpose, but purposely is the safer choice for that meaning.

entries.meaning: On purpose; deliberately, not by accident. ---
examples: He purposely left his phone at home so no one could reach him.
Investigators say the fire was set purposely.
I purposely didn't invite her.
entries.form: -ly from the noun purpose, as in on purpose
entries.contrast: purposely = on purpose (нарочно): I purposely didn't call him. Do not confuse it with purposefully, which describes determined action: She walked purposefully to the stage.

entries.meaning: In other words; said another way. ---
examples: Sales fell by half. Put differently, we lost a million dollars.
Put differently, the problem isn't the price but the quality.
Or, put another way, nobody wants to pay for it.
entries.type: linking — rephrasing what was just said

entries.meaning: In a charmingly old-fashioned or unusual way. ---
examples: The inn is quaintly decorated with antique quilts.
My grandmother quaintly calls the refrigerator the icebox.
The town has a quaintly old-fashioned main street.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle; also mid

entries.meaning: In terms of kind or quality rather than amount. ---
examples: Online classes are qualitatively different from classes in person.
The researchers analyzed the interviews qualitatively.
This isn't just a bigger problem — it's a qualitatively new one.
entries.type: viewpoint; also manner — in terms of kind or quality
entries.position: any position — before an adjective (qualitatively different); end after a verb
entries.contrast: Russian качественно often means well made or done to a high standard (качественно сделано = well made). English qualitatively only means in terms of kind or quality rather than amount: qualitatively different.

entries.meaning: In terms of amount or number; using numbers and measurement. ---
examples: The effect is hard to measure quantitatively.
Quantitatively, the two groups were about the same size.
We need to show quantitatively that the program works.
entries.type: viewpoint; also manner — in terms of amount
entries.position: any position — end after a verb; front with a comma as viewpoint

entries.meaning: In a complaining, whining way. ---
examples: "Why do we always have to leave so early?" he asked querulously.
The old man complained querulously about the noise.
"Are we there yet?" a small voice asked querulously from the back seat.

entries.meaning: In a way that makes people doubt that something is honest, legal or right. ---
examples: The deal was questionably legal at best.
The article relies on questionably sourced statistics.
The money was spent questionably on trips and dinners.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle (questionably legal)

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are asking something or are unsure. ---
examples: She looked at me questioningly.
He raised his eyebrows questioningly.
"Tomorrow?" she asked, glancing questioningly at her husband.

entries.meaning: Fast; at high speed, or after only a short time. ---
examples: She quickly realized she was on the wrong bus.
Don't eat so quickly!
The fire spread more quickly than anyone expected.
entries.type: manner; also time — after a short time
entries.comparison: more/most — more quickly, most quickly; informally quicker, quickest
entries.contrast: In everyday speech the flat forms quick, quicker and quickest often replace quickly: Come quick!, It'll go quicker if we both help. In writing, use quickly and more quickly. fast never takes -ly: He ran fast, not fastly.

entries.meaning: Quietly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Please close the door quietly.
The kids were playing quietly in their room.
"I'm sorry," he said quietly.
The company quietly dropped the product from its lineup.
She's quietly confident about the election.
He quietly retired after thirty years at the bank.

senses.head: Making little or no noise
examples: Please close the door quietly.
The kids were playing quietly in their room.
"I'm sorry," he said quietly.

senses.head: Calmly and without attracting attention or fuss
examples: The company quietly dropped the product from its lineup.
She's quietly confident about the election.
He quietly retired after thirty years at the bank.

entries.meaning: In a noble and idealistic but unrealistic way. ---
examples: He quixotically ran for president with no money and no staff.
She fought quixotically to save the old theater from demolition.
The group quixotically hopes to end all traffic in the city.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are puzzled or slightly amused. ---
examples: The dog tilted its head and looked at me quizzically.
She raised an eyebrow quizzically.
He stared quizzically at the strange device.

entries.meaning: In terms of race; because of a person's race. ---
examples: Our school is very racially diverse.
Police said the attack was racially motivated.
Many neighborhoods in the city are still racially segregated.
entries.русский: по расовому признаку, в расовом отношении
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle (racially diverse, racially motivated)

entries.meaning: In a way that shows great happiness or looks bright and beautiful. ---
examples: The bride smiled radiantly as she walked down the aisle.
She looked radiantly happy after the baby was born.
The sun shone radiantly on the fresh snow.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (radiantly happy)

entries.meaning: Completely and in a basic, very important way. ---
examples: The internet radically changed the way we shop.
Their views on immigration are radically different.
The new design is radically simpler than the old one.
entries.position: before its word — also mid and end (changed radically)

entries.meaning: Raggedly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was breathing raggedly after the long run.
The team played raggedly in the first half.
The crowd sang the anthem raggedly but loudly.
The children were thin and raggedly dressed.
A raggedly clothed man was sleeping on the bench.

senses.head: Unevenly or roughly; not smoothly or in a controlled way
examples: He was breathing raggedly after the long run.
The team played raggedly in the first half.
The crowd sang the anthem raggedly but loudly.

senses.head: In old, torn clothes
examples: The children were thin and raggedly dressed.
A raggedly clothed man was sleeping on the bench.

entries.position: end — also before a participle (raggedly dressed)

entries.meaning: In a dashing, stylish and slightly careless way. ---
examples: He wore his hat tilted rakishly to one side.
The pirate grinned rakishly at the crowd.
His scarf was thrown rakishly over one shoulder.
entries.position: end — mostly after tilted, worn, angled
entries.modifies: verbs and participles (a hat tilted rakishly)

entries.meaning: In a way that spreads or grows quickly and cannot be controlled — usually of something bad. ---
examples: Weeds grew rampantly in the empty lot.
Rumors spread rampantly on social media.
The old regime was rampantly corrupt.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (rampantly corrupt)
entries.modifies: verbs of spreading and growing; adjectives

entries.meaning: Without a plan, pattern or reason; by chance. ---
examples: Winners will be randomly selected from all entries.
He clicked randomly on links for hours.
The chairs were scattered randomly around the room.
entries.position: end — also mid and before a participle (randomly selected)

entries.meaning: Very quickly; at a fast rate. ---
examples: The town is growing rapidly.
Prices rose rapidly after the war started.
Her condition got worse rapidly overnight.

entries.meaning: With great delight or enthusiasm. ---
examples: The audience applauded rapturously at the end of the show.
Her first album was rapturously received by critics.
Fans greeted the team rapturously at the airport.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (rapturously received)

entries.meaning: Too quickly, without thinking about the results. ---
examples: I rashly promised to finish the whole project by Monday.
Don't act rashly — sleep on it.
He rashly spent his savings on a new truck.

entries.meaning: Based on reason and clear thinking, not emotion. ---
examples: It's hard to think rationally when you're this angry.
Let's discuss this calmly and rationally.
People don't always behave rationally with money.

entries.meaning: In a loud, rough, noisy way. ---
examples: The fans cheered raucously after the touchdown.
A group of teenagers laughed raucously at the back of the bus.
Crows were cawing raucously outside my window.

entries.meaning: In an extremely hungry way. ---
examples: I was ravenously hungry after the hike.
The kids ate ravenously when they got home.
The puppy attacked its food ravenously.
entries.modifies: verbs of eating; the adjective hungry

entries.meaning: Extremely, in a way that delights — used of beauty. ---
examples: She looked ravishingly beautiful in the red dress.
The film is ravishingly photographed.
The garden is ravishingly lovely in June.
entries.position: before its word — mostly before beautiful

entries.meaning: Readily has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The drug is readily available at any pharmacy.
Parts for older cars are not readily found.
The answer isn't readily apparent.
She readily agreed to help us move.
He readily admitted that he'd made a mistake.

senses.head: Easily; without difficulty or delay
examples: The drug is readily available at any pharmacy.
Parts for older cars are not readily found.
The answer isn't readily apparent.

senses.head: Willingly; without hesitating
examples: She readily agreed to help us move.
He readily admitted that he'd made a mistake.

entries.position: mid — also before an adjective (readily available)

entries.meaning: Realistically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Realistically, we won't be done before June.
How much can we realistically save each month?
Realistically, the team has no chance of making the playoffs.
The fight scenes were filmed very realistically.
The fruit in the painting is so realistically done that you want to eat it.

senses.head: Being practical about what can actually happen — used to give an honest assessment
examples: Realistically, we won't be done before June.
How much can we realistically save each month?
Realistically, the team has no chance of making the playoffs.

senses.head: In a way that looks or seems real or true to life
examples: The fight scenes were filmed very realistically.
The fruit in the painting is so realistically done that you want to eat it.

entries.position: any position — front with a comma as stance; mid (can realistically); end as manner

entries.meaning: In a way that makes someone feel less worried. ---
examples: The nurse smiled at me reassuringly.
"Everything will be fine," he said reassuringly.
The instructions are reassuringly simple.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (reassuringly simple)

entries.meaning: In a way that openly resists authority or rules. ---
examples: She rebelliously dyed her hair green the week before graduation.
The teenager stared back at his father rebelliously.
A few players rebelliously ignored the coach's curfew.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object

entries.meaning: In a way that each side does or gives the same to the other; mutually. ---
examples: The two countries agreed to recognize each other's licenses reciprocally.
Trust and respect are reciprocally connected.
The two schools reciprocally share their library resources.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (reciprocally linked)

entries.meaning: Without caring about danger or the results of what you do. ---
examples: He was charged with driving recklessly through a school zone.
She spent her savings recklessly on things she didn't need.
The company recklessly ignored the safety warnings.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; also mid

entries.meaning: In a way that can be recognized or clearly identified. ---
examples: The old neighborhood was still recognizably the same.
Even as a sketch, the face was recognizably hers.
Twenty years later, the town was still recognizably the place I grew up in.
entries.position: before its word — usually before an adjective (recognizably human)

entries.meaning: In the act of doing something wrong. ---
examples: The security camera caught him red-handed taking cash from the register.
My little brother was caught red-handed with his hand in the cookie jar.
Police caught the thieves red-handed loading the stolen TVs into a van.
entries.position: end — after catch and its object

entries.meaning: In a quiet, thoughtful way. ---
examples: He sipped his coffee reflectively and looked out the window.
"I guess we all changed that year," she said reflectively.
The old man nodded reflectively at the question.

entries.meaning: In a way that is pleasantly different from what is usual. ---
examples: The new mayor is refreshingly honest about the city's problems.
The menu was refreshingly simple.
It was refreshingly cool by the lake after a week of heat.
entries.type: degree — praises something as a welcome change
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (refreshingly honest)

entries.meaning: In a grand, dignified way, like a king or queen. ---
examples: She walked regally down the staircase in her gown.
The cat sat regally on the windowsill, ignoring us.
The hotel lobby was regally decorated in red and gold.

entries.meaning: In or by a particular region rather than the whole country. ---
examples: The band is popular regionally but unknown nationwide.
Prices for gas vary regionally.
The chain is regionally owned and operated.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective or participle (regionally known)

entries.meaning: With a feeling of sadness or disappointment about something. ---
examples: She regretfully turned down the job offer.
He looked regretfully at the empty box of pizza.
We regretfully informed the staff that the office would close.
entries.position: mid or end — also front with a comma
entries.contrast: Strictly, regretfully describes how a person feels (She regretfully declined = с сожалением отказалась), and regrettably comments on the situation (Regrettably, the flight was canceled = к сожалению). Many Americans use regretfully in the second way too, but careful writers keep them apart.

entries.meaning: Without stopping or becoming less strong or determined. ---
examples: The reporters questioned him relentlessly about the scandal.
It rained relentlessly for three days.
She is relentlessly optimistic, even on bad days.
entries.position: end — also mid, and before an adjective (relentlessly positive)

entries.meaning: Reliably has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My old truck still runs reliably after 200,000 miles.
The test reliably detects the virus within an hour.
The trains here run reliably on time.
We've been reliably told that the deal is off.
The senator was reliably reported to be considering a run for governor.

senses.head: In a way that can be trusted to work or happen as expected
examples: My old truck still runs reliably after 200,000 miles.
The test reliably detects the virus within an hour.
The trains here run reliably on time.

senses.head: From a source that can be trusted, in reliably told and reliably reported
examples: We've been reliably told that the deal is off.
The senator was reliably reported to be considering a run for governor.

entries.position: end — after the verb; mid in reliably reported

entries.meaning: Religiously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He checks the stock market religiously every morning.
She follows the recipe religiously.
We watched that show religiously every Sunday night.
The town is religiously diverse.
Her parents were religiously observant and never worked on the Sabbath.

senses.head: Very regularly and carefully, as if it were a duty
examples: He checks the stock market religiously every morning.
She follows the recipe religiously.
We watched that show religiously every Sunday night.

senses.head: In a way connected with religion
examples: The town is religiously diverse.
Her parents were religiously observant and never worked on the Sabbath.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; mid for the religion sense (religiously observant)

entries.meaning: Without wanting to do something; unwillingly. ---
examples: He reluctantly agreed to drive us to the airport.
She handed over her phone reluctantly.
Reluctantly, the board voted to raise tuition again.
entries.position: mid or end — also front with a comma

entries.meaning: Without pity, or without ever stopping or easing. ---
examples: The villain remorselessly destroyed everyone who stood in his way.
The desert sun beat down remorselessly.
The new manager was remorselessly efficient.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (remorselessly efficient)

entries.meaning: Remotely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Half of our team works remotely now.
The drone can be controlled remotely from a laptop.
The technician fixed my computer remotely.
I'm not remotely interested in golf.
Is it even remotely possible that he's telling the truth?
Nothing he said was remotely funny.

senses.head: From a distance, not in the same place
examples: Half of our team works remotely now.
The drone can be controlled remotely from a laptop.
The technician fixed my computer remotely.

senses.head: Even slightly, in negatives, questions and conditions
examples: I'm not remotely interested in golf.
Is it even remotely possible that he's telling the truth?
Nothing he said was remotely funny.

entries.position: end — in the distance sense; before its word in the degree sense
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives in negatives and questions

entries.meaning: Without paying rent. ---
examples: My cousin lived in our basement rent-free for two years.
The city lets the nonprofit use the building rent-free.
That argument has been living rent-free in my head all week.
entries.position: end — after live, stay or use

entries.meaning: In a way that repeats the same thing again and again. ---
examples: Workers on the line move their wrists repetitively for hours.
The song uses the same four notes repetitively.
The dog barked repetitively until someone opened the door.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows disapproval or disappointment. ---
examples: His mother looked at him reproachfully when he came home late.
"You promised you'd call," she said reproachfully.
The dog stared reproachfully at its empty bowl.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you disapprove of what someone has done. ---
examples: The librarian looked at us reprovingly over her glasses.
"That's not how we talk in this house," her father said reprovingly.
She wagged her finger reprovingly at the dog.

entries.meaning: According to what people say or believe, though it may not be proven. ---
examples: The house is reputedly haunted.
He is reputedly one of the richest men in Texas.
The bar was reputedly a favorite of Al Capone.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.form: -ly from reputed; the -ed is a separate syllable

entries.meaning: In a way that shows anger at being treated unfairly. ---
examples: He resentfully handed over the car keys.
"Nobody ever asks me," she muttered resentfully.
The younger kids watched resentfully as their brother got a new bike.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you accept something bad because you cannot change it. ---
examples: He sighed resignedly and started washing the dishes.
"Fine, we'll take the bus," she said resignedly.
The passengers waited resignedly for another delayed flight.
entries.form: -ly from resigned; the -ed is a separate syllable

entries.meaning: In a determined way, without changing your mind. ---
examples: She resolutely refused to answer the question.
He walked resolutely toward the principal's office.
The governor remained resolutely opposed to the new tax.
entries.position: end — also mid, and before an adjective (resolutely opposed)

entries.meaning: In a very clear and complete way, especially of a win, defeat or answer. ---
examples: Voters resoundingly rejected the proposal.
The home team was resoundingly defeated, 42 to 7.
The bill passed resoundingly, 88 to 11.
entries.type: degree — says a result was clear and decisive
entries.position: before its word — before a participle or adjective (resoundingly defeated); also end

entries.meaning: In a way that is socially acceptable, or good enough though not excellent. ---
examples: He was respectably dressed in a suit and tie.
Our team didn't win, but we finished respectably in fourth place.
The movie did respectably at the box office.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before an adjective in respectably dressed

entries.meaning: In a polite way that shows respect. ---
examples: The students listened respectfully to the veteran's story.
I respectfully disagree with the committee's decision.
Please treat the other players respectfully.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with respectively (соответственно, in the order given). Respectfully is about politeness: I respectfully disagree; Respectfully yours at the end of a formal letter.

entries.meaning: In the same order as the things already mentioned. ---
examples: Maria and Jake finished first and second, respectively.
The shirts cost $15 and $25 respectively.
Revenue and profit rose 8% and 3%, respectively.
entries.type: linking — matches two lists item by item
entries.position: end — after the second list, often with a comma before it
entries.contrast: Respectively only means 'in the same order as the list just given': Ann and Tom are 10 and 12, respectively. Russian соответственно also means 'so, therefore' (Он опоздал, соответственно, мы ушли) — that is so or accordingly, never respectively. And it is not respectfully (уважительно).

entries.meaning: In a sensible way that can be trusted and does not cause harm. ---
examples: Please drink responsibly.
The kids behaved responsibly while we were away.
We want to use public money more responsibly.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you cannot stay still or relax. ---
examples: He tossed and turned restlessly all night.
The crowd shifted restlessly as the concert started late.
She paced restlessly around the waiting room.

entries.meaning: At the ordinary price paid by shoppers, not in bulk. ---
examples: The factory sells retail on weekends and wholesale during the week.
Never buy furniture retail if you can wait for a sale.
Bought retail, those tires would cost twice as much.
entries.position: end — after buy, sell or cost
entries.form: flat — the same form as the noun and adjective retail
entries.contrast: The same word is a noun (She works in retail), an adjective (retail price) and a verb (It retails for $20 = продаётся по цене $20). Only buy retail, sell retail is the adverb. The opposite is wholesale (оптом).

entries.meaning: So that it takes effect from a date in the past. ---
examples: The raise will be paid retroactively to January 1.
The new law cannot be applied retroactively.
The school retroactively changed his grade after the review.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; also mid

entries.meaning: When looking back at the past, or applied to the past. ---
examples: Retrospectively, it's clear that the warning signs were there.
The data was analyzed retrospectively from hospital records.
The rule was applied retrospectively to last year's contracts.
entries.position: end — also front with a comma

entries.meaning: With deep respect, often of a religious kind. ---
examples: The visitors spoke reverently inside the cathedral.
He reverently unwrapped his grandfather's old medal.
The fans stood reverently in front of the statue.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object

entries.meaning: As a question or statement that expects no real answer, or in terms of persuasive speech. ---
examples: "Who needs sleep anyway?" she asked rhetorically.
I was asking rhetorically — you don't have to answer.
Rhetorically, the speech was brilliant, even if the facts were thin.
entries.type: manner; also viewpoint (Rhetorically, the speech worked)
entries.position: end — after ask or say; front with a comma as a viewpoint adverb

entries.meaning: With a regular, repeated pattern of sound or movement. ---
examples: The crowd clapped rhythmically to the music.
Waves beat rhythmically against the pier.
She breathed slowly and rhythmically to calm down.

entries.meaning: Richly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The hall was richly decorated with gold and velvet.
The painting is richly detailed.
The stew is richly flavored with garlic and red wine.
The award was richly deserved.
Her years of hard work were richly rewarded.

senses.head: In a lavish, colorful or full way
examples: The hall was richly decorated with gold and velvet.
The painting is richly detailed.
The stew is richly flavored with garlic and red wine.

senses.head: Fully and properly, in richly deserved and richly rewarded
examples: The award was richly deserved.
Her years of hard work were richly rewarded.

entries.position: before its word — before a participle (richly decorated); also end

entries.meaning: To an unreasonable or silly degree; extremely. ---
examples: Rent in this city is ridiculously expensive.
The test was ridiculously easy.
He showed up ridiculously early for the interview.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb (ridiculously expensive)

entries.meaning: Immediately, without delay. ---
examples: I'll call you back right away.
We knew right away that something was wrong.
If you see smoke, leave the building right away.
entries.contrast: Right here means directly, not correctly. British English also says straight away; Americans say right away.
